demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Leila is a 31-year-old social media manager who lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a midsized city. She came to therapy six months after the accident, though she had been telling herself she was fine for most of that time. The accident happened in late March, on a Tuesday evening. Leila had been working late, monitoring engagement metrics on a client's campaign, and she was rushing home because her ex-husband was supposed to drop off some of her things. She took a shortcut through a residential street she rarely used. Her phone buzzed with a notification-a brand alert from the client-and she glanced down just long enough to read the subject line. When she looked up, a man was crossing the street in front of her car, not at a crosswalk, but close enough that she should have seen him. She hit the brake, but too late. The impact was a single, flat thud, and then the terrible silence of the engine idling while she sat frozen behind the wheel. The man-his name was Marcus, she would learn later-was thrown onto the hood and then onto the pavement. He survived, but with a traumatic brain injury that left him with permanent cognitive deficits. Leila's blood alcohol was zero, her phone records showed she was not texting, but the police report noted the glancing-at-a-notification as a contributing factor. She was not charged.

In the weeks that followed, everything changed. Leila could not stop smelling the inside of her car after the accident: a mix of hot metal, the faint sweetness of spilled coffee from the cup holder, and something metallic and organic that she later realized might have been blood, though she never saw any. That smell returned without warning-when she opened a can of soda, when she walked past a body shop, sometimes for no reason at all. She began to dread being touched unexpectedly. A colleague patted her shoulder to get her attention and she flinched so hard she knocked a cup of water across her desk. She started sitting with her back to the wall in meetings, and she avoided elevators and crowded hallways at work because people pressed too close. At home, she found herself jumping at the sound of her own cat brushing against her leg.

Her job became a minefield. As a social media manager, she was required to monitor comments, respond to brand mentions, and schedule posts. But every time her phone buzzed with a notification-the same sound that had preceded the accident-her heart slammed into her throat and she felt a surge of pure alarm, even though she knew it was just a client request. She started muting notifications entirely and checking her phone only at designated times, but that made her miss real-time engagement opportunities, and her supervisor noticed. More than once, she reacted as if she were about to be attacked when nothing was wrong: rising from her desk, scanning the room, hands shaking. Her colleagues began to whisper about how jumpy she had become. She stopped going out for lunch with them, preferring to eat at her desk with headphones on.

The worst part, she told herself, was how hollow she felt when she tried to remember the accident. Sometimes she could recall the moment in perfect, sensory detail-the sound of the impact, the smell, the way Marcus's body seemed to bounce-but she felt nothing. She described it as watching a movie of someone else's life. That scared her more than the guilt, because it made her wonder if she was a sociopath. Other times, she knew exactly what had happened, but when she tried to tell anyone about it, the words would not come. She would open her mouth to describe the accident and end up sitting in silence, her mind blank, as if the language had been erased. She stopped talking about it altogether.

The divorce had already been finalized before the accident, but Leila had been on reasonably good terms with her ex-husband. After the accident, she withdrew completely. She cancelled plans with friends, stopped responding to texts, and spent her evenings in the dark scrolling through the social media feeds of people who seemed untouched by anything terrible. She believed she could no longer trust herself to make good decisions-she had looked at a phone for two seconds and ruined a man's life. What kind of person did that? The person she used to be-confident, quick to laugh, decisive-felt like a stranger. She looked in the mirror and saw someone else, someone who had permanently damaged not only Marcus but also the future she might have had. She was certain she had changed for the worse, that this was now her real self: a woman who could not be trusted behind a wheel or a phone, who needed to be careful every second, who could never be forgiven.

What finally brought Leila to therapy was not the guilt or the numbness or the startle, but the smell. Three nights before her first appointment, she was chopping an onion for dinner and the scent triggered such a vivid, involuntary flashback that she dropped the knife and stood in the middle of her kitchen, sobbing, with no idea why. She realised she could not keep living this way, that her life had become unrecognisable. She hoped, vaguely, that therapy might give her back the version of herself she lost on that Tuesday in March. But she also feared, privately, that no amount of talking could undo what she had done, and that the person she had become was all she would ever be.
